---
title: Running a Sweep
llms-description: "Launching a run, what one turn of the supervision loop does, arming the timer that guarantees those turns happen with nobody watching, and pausing."
---

## Overview

Running a sweep under Steward is three things, and only the first is a
foreground act:

``` bash
steward launch          # commit what should run, start it, arm the timer
steward timer status    # confirm something will keep tending it
steward status          # ask how it is going, whenever you like
```

Everything between the first and the last happens without you. This page is
about the machinery that makes that true.

## `steward launch`

`launch` is the only verb that reads your definition. It captures the manifest,
reports what committing it would change, commits it as **desired state**, spawns
the first workers, arms a timer, and returns.

It deliberately does not block. The thing supervising the run is not the
terminal you typed into — if it were, closing your laptop would end the sweep.

Because `launch` is what commits desired state, it is also how you *change* a
run: edit the definition, launch again. See [Amending a Run](amending.qmd).

## What a turn does

``` bash
steward tend
```

One turn — a **tend** — compares the manifest against the log directory and
closes the gap:

1.  **Observe.** Read the log directory's headers and sweep the process table
    for live workers.
2.  **Decide.** Work out which tasks need a worker, which finished, which died,
    and which the definition no longer asks for.
3.  **Act.** Spawn, reap, archive.
4.  **Record.** Rewrite `status.md` and append what it observed to the journal.

Three properties make that safe to put on a timer, and they are worth trusting
rather than working around:

|  |  |
|----|----|
| **A repeated turn is a no-op.** | Tend twice in a row and the second does nothing. There is no harm in an extra one. |
| **An interrupted turn is repaired by the next.** | Kill a tend halfway through and nothing is left inconsistent — the following turn observes whatever actually happened and proceeds from there. |
| **A turn never blocks.** | Anything whose duration is unbounded is spawned as a detached child that some later turn observes. A tend returns in seconds. |

That last one is why a missed turn is not a stall. Workers execute continuously
between turns; what a late turn delays is the *scheduling of new work*, not the
progress of work already running.

### One task, one process

Steward spawns exactly one worker per task — always, not by default. Two
reasons, and the first is the binding one:

-   **The GIL.** Evals are mostly I/O-bound, but the work that is *not* waiting
    — transcript construction, JSON serialization, `.eval` compression,
    non-model scorers — is all Python bytecode, and it serializes within a
    process however high sample concurrency goes. One process saturates one
    core.
-   **Failure isolation.** One crash costs one task.

Workers are spawned **detached**, so the run survives Steward exiting, your
shell closing, or the machine you launched from going to sleep.

### How many run at once

The ceiling is **10 concurrent workers** by default, and you are expected to
raise it once a run is behaving:

``` yaml
---
max_workers: 24
---
```

in [`_steward.md`](directives.qmd), or `--max-workers` for one turn. It is a
resource guard — memory, file descriptors, how much simultaneous spike a box
should be asked to absorb — rather than a parallelism budget, which is why it is
a flat number rather than something derived from your core count. Ten workers on
four cores is entirely ordinary: a worker is on the CPU in bursts and waiting on
a model API in between.

Anything past the ceiling queues. Steward spawns **task-major** — every model
for the first task, then every model for the second — rather than in the order
enumeration happens to produce, which is model-major. That matters for a reason
that only shows up when a run is interrupted: stop a model-major sweep halfway
and one model is complete and the other untouched, so the arms cannot be
compared at all. Task-major means a halted run is still a comparison. It also
spreads load across several rate-limit buckets instead of hammering one.

### Errors are counted, not fixed

Workers run with `fail_on_error=False`, so a task always reaches the end of its
dataset and finishes carrying whatever errored samples remain. A sample gets the
`retry_on_error` attempts your definition asked for, and that is the **only**
automatic recovery tier — every further attempt, at sample or task level, is a
decision rather than a rule Steward executes.

The consequence is that Steward never restarts a failed task on its own. A task
that fails despite `fail_on_error=False` has failed structurally — a bad import,
an OOM, a scorer that throws — and respawning a definition that will not import
spends money to arrive where it started. A task that has stopped getting
anywhere is reported as needing attention instead ([Reading
Status](status.qmd)).

## The timer

A tend has to happen whether or not anyone is around to type it, and nothing
else in the design guarantees that. So arming a timer is part of starting a run
rather than a step in a checklist somebody remembers.

``` bash
steward timer arm                    # detect a scheduler and install
steward timer arm --interval 5m      # override _steward.md's interval
steward timer arm --scheduler cron   # override the detected scheduler
steward timer status                 # ask the scheduler what is really there
steward timer disarm                 # remove it
```

Steward hands the job to something the machine already runs, preferring what
survives the most:

| scheduler | | survives |
|----|----|----|
| `launchd` | macOS user agent | a reboot |
| `systemd` | user timer | a reboot |
| `cron` | a marked block in your crontab | a logout |

All three survive the terminal you armed from, which is the property that
matters. **Detection is allowed to fail.** A machine with none of the three is
told so rather than quietly given something weaker, and running unsupervised
stays available as an explicit choice — which has the merit of making an
unsupervised run *look* unsupervised.

Detection also depends on the interval rather than only on the machine: a
seven-minute interval is not expressible in a crontab, so a host where cron is
the only scheduler will take `10m` and refuse `7m`.

Arming is idempotent: an existing timer is removed first, so re-arming at a new
interval or under a different scheduler leaves exactly one. What a scheduled
tend prints before Steward can log anything of its own goes to `timer.log` in
the workspace, and `arm` says so.

### Arming checks that a scheduled tend can authenticate

A timer does not inherit your shell, and the failure that produces is the worst
kind available here: every interval all night, a worker starts, authenticates
against nothing, and writes a log saying so, while `status.md` reports a fleet
dutifully trying.

So arming compares two environments — what your shell holds against what the
workspace's `.env` holds — and **refuses** when a credential is in the first and
not the second, because that is exactly a credential that will be gone at 02:00.
The remedy it suggests is to put the key in that `.env`, which is the file the
workers already read and which `init` has already gitignored for you.

It is a diff, not a requirement. Steward does not know which provider your
definition uses and does not guess: a required-key list would refuse correct
setups and miss unusual ones. No value ever leaves the check either — resolving
a `.env` line is the only way to know whether a key will really be there, so
values are read and only names come back. Use `--no-env-check` to arm anyway
when you know better.

### A run says when nothing is tending it

A scheduler cannot report its own absence, so arming writes down what it
installed, and any turn that finds no tend for two intervals reports the run as
**unsupervised**. That catches a crontab somebody rewrote as readily as one
Steward removed.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
`steward timer status` is the one command that asks the scheduler directly.
Everything else — a tend, a `status`, the attention list — goes on what arming
recorded, because those run every few minutes and asking costs a subprocess.
:::

## Pausing

``` bash
steward pause --reason "provider incident, waiting it out"
steward resume
```

Pausing means **stop scheduling**. Every later turn reports the run as paused
and spawns nothing; workers already in flight are left alone to finish, because
stopping one is not a mechanical act and it is not what pausing means.

The pause is recorded in the journal rather than in disposable state, so
clearing Steward's cache cannot silently resume an expensive run. On resume, the
next turn converges from whatever it finds — which is not necessarily where the
run was when you paused it, since logs landed and workers exited in the
meantime. That is the ordinary behaviour of the loop rather than a caveat about
pausing.

Note the distinction from disarming the timer. `disarm` stops anything happening
without somebody typing it, including the reaping and reporting that make a
paused run legible; `pause` keeps the loop running and tells it not to start
work.

## Two Stewards cannot collide

A tend takes a short-lived lock before it writes anything, held for the seconds
the turn runs. So a timer and an agent tending at the same moment is a non-event
— two callers of the same function, serialized.

If a tend crashes, the lock is released by the operating system, and the next
turn simply takes it. If one *wedges* — alive but stuck — it is killed and the
lock taken, because a wedged supervisor blocking its own replacement is worse
than a dead one, and escalating to a human at 2am is worth nothing when the
whole premise is that nobody is there. `steward tend --no-break-claim` inverts
that for when you are attached and would rather examine the wedge.

Killing a tend destroys no work: workers are detached and outlive it, and every
write a turn makes is built to be interrupted.
